# THEORYs with `tags` `endosymbiosis`

*Topics — What a work is about. Nucleation holds whatever reading the owner files here, whether or not an Anthology of the SOTA topic could also hold it; instruction for ML practice belongs to the anthology (ADR-048). The words are seeded from the clusters the reading-time triage of 2026-09-25 found, and grow by decision.*

**Endosymbiosis and reductive evolution** — how one organism comes to live inside another and depend on it, and how that ends — reductive genome evolution by drift, deletional bias or adaptive loss (including the Black Queen dependencies of free-living microbes), complementary loss across partners, nested symbioses and symbiont splitting and replacement, endosymbiotic gene transfer, protein import and host control of transmission, organellogenesis and organelle loss, and eukaryogenesis. The ecology of a partnership is ecology (ADR-055).

| [THEORY-1048](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1048.md) v2 | Leaky functions are lost by individual selection | Morris, Lenski & Zinser (2012), [LIT-1568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1568.md), read in [NOTE-1212](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1212.md). A loss-of-function mutant invades when its resource saving B = (Q_A − Q_M)/Q_A exceeds its cost C, which falls as other cells' leaky activity protects it. Because protection falls as producers become rare, the loss is frequency dependent and stops short of community-wide loss. The evidence is Prochlorococcus's loss of katG and its dependence on a peroxide-removing community. The dependence it produces is one-way, from beneficiaries to helpers, and involves no collective. | Active |
| [THEORY-1049](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1049.md) v3 | Tiny symbionts lose envelope, then translation | McCutcheon, Garber, Spencer & Warren (2024), [LIT-1571](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1571.md), read in [NOTE-1213](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1213.md). The envelope goes first, near 400 kb, and translation starts to go below about 200 kb, the authors' "tipping point". Such symbionts have three-membrane envelopes and among the most biased proteomes in bacteria. They can only work if the host provides what they no longer encode. The host's role is inferred, not shown: the mechanisms are, in the paper's word, mysteries. | Active |
| [THEORY-1050](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1050.md) v2 | Dependence-first bias rests on one mapping | Athreya, Czuppon & Gokhale (2025), [LIT-1570](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1570.md), read in [NOTE-1211](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1211.md). In the exponential version of the model, all four traits rise monotonically. Each partner becomes more obligate than adhesive, because a gain in adhesion is "damped by the other adhesion" in the dissociation rate. Table S1 shows this is a consequence of that mapping: matched mappings give no bias, and the opposite mapping biases trajectories towards cohesion. The record's summary of the result, "even when investments are uncorrelated", is true of the traits' genetic correlation but not of their functional coupling, which is what decides it. | Active |
| [THEORY-1051](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1051.md) v3 | Mutual dependence is parameter-bound, not default | Athreya, Czuppon & Gokhale (2025), [LIT-1570](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1570.md), read in [NOTE-1211](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1211.md). With the symbiont's population larger and faster, its obligacy reaches 1 first. In the base model the host's R₀ is then exactly 1, so host obligacy is neutral. With within-collective deaths the host goes fully obligate, and with within-collective births it goes back to independence. Obligacy rose from zero in simulations where the collective's carrying capacity exceeded about aK_HK_S/d, a condition shown sufficient, not necessary; collective growth rate does not matter. The authors take the model as a null: a transition "is far from an inevitable outcome of the existence of a higher level of selection". | Active |
| [THEORY-1098](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1098.md) v2 | Mitochondrion lost only after functions moved | Karnkowska et al. (2019), [LIT-1574](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1574.md), read in [NOTE-1243](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1243.md). The SUF replacement of the mitochondrial Fe–S pathway is shared by all examined Preaxostyla, including relatives that keep a mitochondrion-related organelle, and those relatives' organelle still houses the glycine cleavage system that M. exilis lacks. So the organelle lost its jobs in at least two steps before it was lost. Apart from the mitochondrion, peroxisomes and mitophagy, the cell's systems are those of an ordinary eukaryote. The order is inferred, not dated, and absence is limited by annotation. | Active |
| [THEORY-1099](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1099.md) v3 | Host complexity predates the mitochondrion | Kay et al. (2026), [LIT-1566](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1566.md), read in [NOTE-1234](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1234.md). A dated species tree places nFECA at 3.05–2.79 Ga, mFECA at 2.37–2.13 Ga and LECA at 1.80–1.67 Ga. Against an endosymbiosis marker at about 2.2 Ga, 85% of archaeal-origin duplications are older, and most non-alphaproteobacterial bacterial duplications are younger. The authors reject mitochondria-early scenarios and argue against serial endosymbiosis. The sharp edges are that duplication dates bound functions from above, that the priors shape which family can be older, and that the authors themselves cannot order phagocytosis and the mitochondrion. | Active |
| [THEORY-1100](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1100.md) v2 | Integration needs no endosymbiont gene transfer | Sørensen, Stiller, Kröninger & Nowack (2025), [LIT-1560](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1560.md), read in [NOTE-1241](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1241.md). Protein mass spectrometry of isolated endosymbionts found hundreds of host proteins imported into Paulinella's chromatophore and more than 350 into the nitroplast, where they fill gaps left by lost genes. In Paulinella the imported proteins come mostly from the host's own genes, with some from gene transfer from the chromatophore and from other bacteria. In the nitroplast no gene transfer from the symbiont has been found at all. So the route to an organelle is import, and the endosymbiont's genes need not move. The origins are stated in summary, not counted, and the import mechanisms are unknown. | Active |
| [THEORY-1101](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1101.md) v3 | Stem length is not an acquisition clock | Tobiasson, Luo, Wolf & Koonin (2026), [LIT-1558](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1558.md), read in [NOTE-1242](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1242.md). They test the stem-length method of Pittis and Gabaldón on their own trees and reproduce its mitochondrion-late signal only for long stems. Below 0.3, where 70% of stems lie, the order reverses, and genes presumably acquired together scatter widely. They conclude that "even normalized stem lengths are determined primarily by factors other than the gene acquisition time". The paper still favours a late mitochondrion, on other grounds. | Active |
| [THEORY-1102](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1102.md) v2 | Mitochondria arrived late to a chimaeric host | Pittis & Gabaldón (2016), [LIT-1595](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1595.md), read in [NOTE-1240](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1240.md). Of 1,078 LECA families, bacterial ones have shorter normalized stems than archaeal ones (P = 1.38e-25), and alphaproteobacterial ones shorter than other bacterial ones (P = 0.044). Origin tracks location: alphaproteobacterial with the mitochondrion, other bacterial with endomembranes, archaeal with the nucleus. A plastid control runs the right way. The sharp edges are that stem length measures distance to the closest sampled relative, so sampling can move it, and that the chimaeric host could have come from partners or from transfer, which the paper cannot tell apart. | Active |
| [THEORY-1103](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1103.md) v2 | Buchnera keeps only what its host lacks | Shigenobu et al. (2000), [LIT-1596](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1596.md), read in [NOTE-1236](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1236.md). The first complete genome of an obligate insect endosymbiont: 640,681 bp, a subset of E. coli's. What is shown is gene content. The interlocking of host and symbiont metabolism is inferred from it and from earlier physiology. That Buchnera cannot live outside the bacteriocyte, and that the host supplies its membrane lipids, are the authors' inferences. The paper names no mechanism of loss beyond a homeostatic niche: it says nothing of drift. | Active |
| [THEORY-1104](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1104.md) v3 | Asgard is the largest eukaryotic gene source | Tobiasson, Luo, Wolf & Koonin (2026), [LIT-1558](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1558.md), read in [NOTE-1242](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1242.md). In 4,290 well-resolved eukaryotic–prokaryotic clusters, Asgard takes 50% of likelihood weight and leads in almost every functional class. Alphaproteobacteria account for mitochondrial translation, oxidative phosphorylation and 4Fe-4S assembly. About a third of clusters point elsewhere, with no functional pattern except a narrow Myxococcota signal. The authors infer a complex Asgard ancestor, a late mitochondrion and "no indication of another symbiotic event". The composition is shown; the scenario is read off it. | Active |
| [THEORY-1105](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1105.md) v3 | LECA acquired partners in serial waves | Bernabeu, Manzano-Morales, Marcet-Houben & Gabaldón (2026), [LIT-1561](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1561.md), read in [NOTE-1237](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1237.md). Under thresholds chosen to maximize assignments to Alphaproteobacteria and Asgard, Myxococcota (3.92% of the proteome) and Planctomycetota (2.24%) pass in every dataset, beside Alphaproteobacteria (3.99%) and Asgard (3.28%). A control removing Alphaproteobacteria from the database does not reproduce their pattern. Stem lengths put Planctomycetota before the mitochondrion. The authors "challenge models depicting eukaryogenesis as a one-off event resulting from a binary symbiotic interaction", and also say their data "do not provide information on the host or endosymbiotic nature of any partner". | Active |
| [THEORY-1106](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1106.md) v2 | Hosts raise titre for fragmented Hodgkinia | Campbell, Łukasik, Meyer, Buckner, Simon, Veloso, Michalik & McCutcheon (2018), [LIT-1590](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1590.md), read in [NOTE-1235](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1235.md). Measured: Hodgkinia cells per egg from 4,889 in a single-lineage cicada to 30,154 in M. septendecim, with Sulcia at 2,572 to 5,643; marker genotypes present in every egg sampled; the same route under the light microscope. Not shown: a trend across complexity beyond M. septendecim, or that splitting came first. The authors also speculate that a larger transmitted population weakens bottlenecks and could feed further splitting. | Active |
| [THEORY-1107](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1107.md) v2 | Organelles arise stepwise via protein import | Sørensen, Stiller, Kröninger & Nowack (2025), [LIT-1560](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1560.md), read in [NOTE-1241](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1241.md). Their closing scenario orders the steps from endosymbiont to organelle: effectors first, then dependence through one redundant imported protein, then many imported proteins once a targeting signal evolves. Rhizobia, targeted by about 700 host peptides yet not vertically transmitted, are their case of control without integration. It is a scenario built from systems at different stages, not a sequence observed in any one. | Active |
| [THEORY-1108](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1108.md) v2 | Asgard ancestor was likely syntrophic | Imachi et al. (2020), [LIT-1591](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1591.md), read in [NOTE-1238](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1238.md). Partner inhibitors impair MK-D1's growth, added hydrogen or formate stops it, and it grows with either of two methanogens, so its dependence is on a service that several partners can supply. Cryo-EM and TEM show no internal compartments. The step from this one organism to the Asgard ancestor is a genomic inference, which the authors hedge. The sharp edge for the record is that the most famous transition in individuality may have begun from a host already dependent on others, with no partner specificity, cohesion or control. | Active |
| [THEORY-1109](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1109.md) v3 | LECA central carbon metabolism was chimeric | Santana-Molina, Williams, Snel & Spang (2025), [LIT-1564](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1564.md), read in [NOTE-1239](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1239.md). LECA had a complete central carbon metabolism. Six enzymes are placed with Asgard archaea, mostly cytosolic (bootstrap 39–97%, two ambiguous). Seventeen are alphaproteobacterial, ten of them in the TCA cycle, mostly mitochondrial. Others come from several bacteria, none dominant. Since LECA, Asgard enzymes have been replaced in many lineages and enzymes retargeted regardless of origin. The authors read the split as support for syntrophy; it does not discriminate syntrophy from other symbiogenetic models. | Active |
